The directory `logs/` holds one TLC run per configuration, and
`expectations.txt` maps each configuration to the verdict it is expected to
produce — witnesses are EXPECTED to violate, because a witness that stops
violating has stopped being evidence.

The verdict rules, exactly: a log VIOLATES iff it contains "is violated." or
"Temporal properties were violated"; it HOLDS iff it contains "No error has
been found."; anything else — parse errors, deadlocks, truncation — is ERROR.

Classify every log, then find the rotted witness: a configuration expected to
violate whose run actually holds. Write answer.txt: one `<name> <verdict>`
line per configuration sorted by name, then a final line `rotted <name>` or
`rotted -` if there is none.

Grading runs against a pristine copy of these files plus your answer.txt.

Retain only what genuinely makes similar future work cheaper:
- a fact or procedure you had to work out (a build quirk, a format rule,

- a transformation you would otherwise write again (a parser, a reshaper,
  a converter): write it as a tool, with the ordinary file tools. A tool is
  a directory .vivarium/tools/<name>/ holding tool.json --

      {"name": "...", "description": "...",
       "exec": ["python3", "run.py"],
       "parameters": [{"name": "...", "type": "string",
                        "description": "...", "required": true}]}

  -- and the script it names. The script reads one JSON object of arguments
  on stdin and prints its result. Later tasks call it by name.

  A tool costs more to write than a note and only pays if you would reach
  for it again, so prefer the note unless the transformation is plainly
  one you would rewrite.
